title: What Hands-On Testing Finds Beyond the Checklist
description: Understand why lived experience with disability and assistive technologies is essential for effective accessibility QA — moving beyond automated checks to meaningful usability.

title: What Accessibility QA Actually Is
description: What an accessibility reviewer produces, who consumes it, which method catches which barrier, and why a reviewer who uses the technology finds different bugs from one who reads about it.

title: How Barriers Get Built
description: Why a barrier is a property of a design, not of the person who meets it — the vocabulary that separates impairment, barrier and disability, the real range of access needs one product has to serve at once, and where in a design process the assumptions that cause barriers actually get made.

title: Reading WCAG Properly
description: How WCAG's four layers — principles, guidelines, success criteria and techniques — actually work, what a conformance claim at Level A, AA or AAA literally asserts, and how to cite the criterion that actually governs a finding instead of the nearest familiar number.

title: The Law Behind the Standard
description: Which legal frameworks actually make accessibility mandatory — EN 301 549 and the European Accessibility Act, the ADA and Section 508 in the US — what each genuinely requires, what an honest accessibility statement contains, and how accessibility gets decided at procurement before a single screen is designed. Not legal advice: the frameworks a reviewer needs to recognise, not a substitute for counsel.

title: What Automated Testing Can and Can't Find
description: Running axe, Lighthouse and a browser's own accessibility inspector — what each actually costs and does when the free tier disappears — the real, bounded share of barriers automation can detect, why the same page produces different scores from different tools, how to tell a false positive from a real finding, and why a green CI check is worth having and easy to over-trust.
